/record/physicalDescription	Low table, huali wood. Chinese; Ming dynasty, 16th century. A low rectangular table of plain polished huali wood, set on square-section legspositioned at the corners. Construction: The top is mitered, mortised and tenoned frame construction with one-piece floating panel. The frame are exposed on the short members. Three transverse stretchers are dovetailed to the underside of the floating panel, and mortised and tenoned into the long members of the frame. The tenons of the outer two stretchers are exposed. The square-section legs are mitered, and double mortised and tenoned into the frame at the corners. They terminate in horsefeet. The legs cut down. Curvilinear, beaded-edge aprons are tongue-and-grooved into the legs on all four sides, the curve on the long sides being more complex. The beading of the aprons runs continously into the beaded edges of the legs. Plain curvilinear stretchers with beaded upper and lower edges are mitered, mortised and tenoned into the legs, connecting them near the top. The underside shows traces of straw, together with evidence of retaining.
